title: Reading the Wisdom Books
summary: Proverbs, Job, and Ecclesiastes: what wisdom meant in Israel and its neighbors, what a proverb is and is not, how the three books argue with each other about how the world works, and how the church came to read Christ as the wisdom of God.

sections.body:
Three books of the Old Testament are usually called the Wisdom Books: Proverbs, Job, and Ecclesiastes. Some add the Song of Songs and a handful of psalms (1, 37, 49, 73, 112, among others) that share their concerns, and Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include two more wisdom books from the centuries before Christ, the Wisdom of Ben Sira (also called Sirach or Ecclesiasticus, written in Hebrew about 180 BC and translated into Greek by the author's grandson after 132 BC) and the Wisdom of Solomon (written in Greek, probably in Alexandria, in the first century BC). The Letter of James is often called the wisdom book of the New Testament.

The Hebrew word for wisdom, chokmah, is broader than the English. It covers the skill of a craftsman (the artisans who built the tabernacle are ‘wise of heart’ in Exodus 31:6), the shrewdness of a counselor, and the moral insight to live well. In the Wisdom Books it means the art of living rightly in God's world: how to speak, work, handle money, raise children, choose friends, stay married, rule justly, and face suffering and death. Wisdom looks at ordinary life, observes how it tends to go, and draws conclusions.

What is striking about these books, compared with the Law and the Prophets, is what is missing. They rarely mention the exodus, Sinai, the covenant, the temple, or the history of Israel. Job is not even an Israelite; he lives in the land of Uz. Wisdom addresses every human being as a creature in a world God made, and it learns from creation, from experience, and from the wisdom of other nations. Yet it is not secular. Proverbs sets its whole program under one sentence: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (Proverbs 1:7), repeated with a variation in 9:10. The fear of the LORD, meaning reverent trust and obedience toward Israel's God, is the first principle from which all real wisdom starts.

Israel's wisdom belonged to a wider conversation. The Bible says so itself: Solomon's wisdom is compared with “all the wisdom of Egypt” and the wise men of the East (1 Kings 4:30-31), and Proverbs includes sayings attributed to two non-Israelites, Agur (Proverbs 30) and King Lemuel, whose mother taught him (Proverbs 31:1-9). Egypt and Mesopotamia had long traditions of instruction literature, in which a father or king passes advice to a son, and of reflective works on suffering and the justice of the gods.

The most famous parallel is the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope, a work from the late second millennium BC (the Ramesside period). In 1924 the Egyptologist Adolf Erman showed that a section of Proverbs, beginning at 22:17 with “Incline your ear and hear the words of the wise”, closely parallels it in content and sometimes in wording, especially in 22:17 to 23:11. Amenemope is arranged in thirty chapters, and Proverbs 22:20 contains a difficult Hebrew word that many scholars, following Erman, read as ‘thirty’, so that the verse refers to ‘thirty sayings’. Most scholars conclude that the Israelite sages knew and adapted Amenemope. Some conservative scholars have argued for a common source rather than direct borrowing. Either way, the adaptation is instructive: the Israelite version sets the borrowed advice under trust in the LORD (22:19).

Other works shed light on Job and Ecclesiastes. A Babylonian poem known by its first line, Ludlul bēl nēmeqi (‘I will praise the lord of wisdom’), probably from the late second millennium BC, tells of a righteous sufferer abandoned by the gods, mocked by friends, and finally restored by Marduk. The so-called Babylonian Theodicy (about 1000 BC) is a dialogue between a sufferer and a friend about divine justice, with an acrostic structure. Egyptian texts such as the Dispute between a Man and His Ba debate whether life is worth living. None of these is the book of Job; the Bible's version differs in its refusal of easy answers and in its God, who speaks. But they show that Israel was not the first to ask these questions, and that the biblical writers answered them in the terms of their own faith.

sections.h: Proverbs: what a proverb is and is not
sections.body:
A proverb is a short, memorable saying that captures something generally true about life. The Hebrew word mashal covers proverbs, comparisons, riddles, and parables, all ways of setting two things beside each other so that one throws light on the other. Proverbs are compressed on purpose. They are not complete accounts of reality; each one catches a single angle, and wisdom lies in knowing which proverb fits the moment.

The book of Proverbs makes this point itself by placing two opposite sayings side by side: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you yourself will be like him.” and “Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he become wise in his own eyes.” (Proverbs 26:4-5). The ancient rabbis noticed the apparent contradiction, and the Talmud (Shabbat 30b) records a debate over whether Proverbs should be withdrawn from use because of it; the answer given was that the two verses apply to different situations. That is the whole method of proverbial wisdom. Both sayings are true, and the wise person discerns which applies.

This means proverbs are not promises or guarantees. “Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it.” (Proverbs 22:6) states how things generally go and urges parents to take training seriously. It does not promise that every child of faithful parents will believe, and reading it as a guarantee has laid heavy and undeserved guilt on many parents. The same is true of the proverbs that tie diligence to wealth: “Idle hands make one poor, but diligent hands bring wealth.” (10:4). Proverbs also knows that the world is not so simple. It says that injustice sweeps away the poor man's field (13:23), and it values righteousness above wealth: “Better a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure with turmoil.” (15:16). The ‘better than’ sayings in particular admit that doing right sometimes costs something.

Proverbs also sets human planning under God's rule. “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD.” (16:33). “A horse is prepared for the day of battle, but victory is of the LORD.” (21:31). The sages expected careful effort and trusted God with the outcome.

The German scholar Klaus Koch argued in 1955 that the Old Testament thinks of an act-consequence connection, in which deeds carry their own results built into them, rather than of God handing out rewards and punishments from outside. Others think Koch drew the line too sharply, since Proverbs also speaks of the LORD repaying. The debate helps readers see that Proverbs is describing the moral grain of a created world, not a vending machine.

Proverbs is a collection of collections, marked by its own headings. Chapters 1 to 9 are long instructions from a father to a son, urging him to choose wisdom and avoid folly, and personifying both as women calling in the streets: Lady Wisdom, who was with God at creation, and the adulterous woman and Lady Folly, whose house leads to death. These chapters are the book's introduction and give the frame for reading the short sayings that follow. Chapters 10 to 22:16 hold the proverbs of Solomon, mostly two-line sayings with little obvious order, though scholars have found clusters linked by catchwords and themes. Patrick Skehan noted that there are 375 of them, the numerical value of the letters of Solomon's name in Hebrew; whether that is design or coincidence is debated.

Then come the words of the wise (22:17 to 24:22, the section related to Amenemope) and a short appendix (24:23-34); further proverbs of Solomon “which were copied by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah” (25:1), which show that the book was still being compiled more than two centuries after Solomon; the words of Agur (chapter 30), with his numerical sayings (‘three things, and four’); the words of King Lemuel (31:1-9); and the closing acrostic poem on the capable woman (31:10-31), who embodies in daily life the wisdom that chapters 1 to 9 personified.

The ‘son’ addressed in the book reflects the setting of family and royal court instruction. It has long been read as addressed to every reader, male and female; the book ends by praising a woman as the model of wisdom in action.

The traditional view attributes the core of the book to Solomon, who is said to have composed three thousand proverbs (1 Kings 4:32), with later additions named in the headings. Most scholars accept that some material may go back to the monarchy, and date the final collection to the Persian period, with chapters 1 to 9 often thought to be among the latest parts. Bruce Waltke's two-volume commentary in the New International Commentary on the Old Testament (2004 and 2005) and Michael V. Fox's two volumes in the Anchor Bible (2000 and 2009) represent careful work from a conservative evangelical and a critical Jewish perspective respectively, and agree on far more than they disagree about in reading the text.

If Proverbs describes how the world generally works, Job asks what happens when it does not. Job is introduced as a man who “was blameless and upright, fearing God and shunning evil” (Job 1:1), the very picture of the wise and righteous person Proverbs commends. In a scene in heaven hidden from Job, the accuser (in Hebrew ha-satan, ‘the adversary’, with the article, so that many scholars read it as a title rather than a name) asks the question the whole book turns on: “Does Job fear God for nothing?” (1:9). Is human piety simply a transaction? Job loses his property, his children, and his health, and the rest of the book tests whether his faith was ever more than a bargain.

The book's structure is part of its meaning. A prose prologue (chapters 1 and 2) and a prose epilogue (42:7-17) frame a long poem. In the poetry, Job curses the day of his birth (chapter 3), and three friends, Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar, answer him in three cycles of speeches (chapters 4 to 27), a poem on wisdom stands alone (28), Job makes his final defense (29 to 31), a younger man named Elihu speaks (32 to 37), and then God answers from the whirlwind (38 to 41), and Job responds (42:1-6).

The friends speak the theology of Proverbs, applied without wisdom. Eliphaz asks, “Who, being innocent, has ever perished?” (4:7). Their reasoning runs backward: the righteous prosper, so if you suffer, you must have sinned. Much of what they say, taken alone, sounds like Scripture, and some of it is quoted in the New Testament (Job 5:13 in 1 Corinthians 3:19). Their error is to turn a general truth into a rule that explains every case. Job, for his part, refuses to confess sins he did not commit, and in his anguish accuses God of injustice. Yet at the end God says to Eliphaz: “you have not spoken about Me accurately, as My servant Job has” (42:7). The man who argued with God, honestly and to his face, is vindicated over the friends who defended God with a formula.

God's speeches from the whirlwind do not explain Job's suffering. They never mention the scene in heaven. Instead they open a vast view of creation, from the foundations of the earth to the wild donkey and the war-horse, Behemoth and Leviathan: “Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?” (38:4). Readers have heard these speeches very differently: as a rebuke to Job's presumption, as an invitation into the wonder and wildness of a world far larger than human justice can measure, or as God's presence itself being the answer. Job's reply, “My ears had heard of You, but now my eyes have seen You.” (42:5), suggests that what changed was not his information but his relationship to God. The next verse is notoriously difficult; the Hebrew can mean that Job despises himself, that he retracts his words, or that he is comforted concerning dust and ashes, and English versions differ accordingly.

The date and authorship of Job are unknown. The story is set in a patriarchal world, with wealth measured in herds and Job offering sacrifice as head of his family, and the Talmud records the view that Moses wrote it, among others. Proposals for its composition range from the time of Solomon to the period after the exile, with many scholars favoring the sixth to fourth centuries BC. The Greek translation of Job is about a sixth shorter than the Hebrew, and fragments of an Aramaic translation of Job were found at Qumran (11QtgJob). Job 13:15 is a well-known case where the Hebrew text itself has two readings: the written text says ‘I will not hope’ or ‘I have no hope’, while the traditional reading tradition says ‘I will hope in him’, which the Berean Standard Bible follows: “Though He slay me, I will hope in Him.”

sections.h: Ecclesiastes: the limits of what we can know
sections.body:
Ecclesiastes presses the question further. Its speaker is Qohelet, a Hebrew title meaning something like ‘one who assembles’ (a congregation, or sayings), rendered Ekklesiastes in Greek and ‘the Teacher’ or ‘the Preacher’ in English. He opens and closes with the same cry, translated in the Berean Standard Bible “Futility of futilities” (Ecclesiastes 1:2 and 12:8). The key word, hebel, appears thirty-eight times in the book. Its basic meaning is breath or vapor; it is the name of Abel, whose life was brief. Jerome's Latin translated it vanitas, which gave the King James Version ‘vanity’. Modern versions use ‘meaningless’ (NIV), ‘futile’ (BSB), ‘fleeting’, or, in Michael Fox's reading, ‘absurd’. The choice of translation shapes the whole book: is life empty, or brief and elusive, or frustratingly beyond human grasp?

Qohelet tests everything under the sun, pleasure, work, wisdom, wealth, and power, and finds that none of it can be held onto, that death comes to wise and fool alike, and that the moral order Proverbs describes does not always hold: “There are righteous men who get what the actions of the wicked deserve, and there are wicked men who get what the actions of the righteous deserve.” (8:14). Yet the book repeatedly turns to joy as God's gift: “Nothing is better for a man than to eat and drink and enjoy his work. I have also seen that this is from the hand of God.” (2:24). It says that God “has also set eternity in the hearts of men, yet they cannot fathom the work that God has done from beginning to end” (3:11). And it closes with a second voice, an editor or frame narrator speaking about Qohelet in the third person (12:9-14), who concludes: “Fear God and keep His commandments, because this is the whole duty of man.” (12:13).

Readers have heard the book in strikingly different ways. Some, such as James Crenshaw (Ecclesiastes, 1987), take Qohelet as a skeptic whose view of God is dark and distant, with the ending added to make the book acceptable. R. N. Whybray, in a 1982 article, called Qohelet a ‘preacher of joy’, stressing the repeated calls to enjoy life as God's gift. Tremper Longman (in his 1998 commentary) and others, building on Michael Fox's work on the frame narrative, read the body of the book as the words of a searching, unsettled Qohelet that the frame narrator presents to his son and then evaluates, so that the book's final word is the narrator's. Derek Kidner (The Message of Ecclesiastes, 1976) and many preachers read Qohelet as deliberately exploring life ‘under the sun’, without the light of revelation, to show that such a life cannot satisfy.

The book's title verse attributes it to “the son of David, king in Jerusalem” (1:1), and Jewish and Christian tradition identified the speaker with Solomon. Most modern scholars, including many conservatives, date the book to the Persian or early Hellenistic period (roughly 450 to 250 BC) because its Hebrew is late, with Persian loanwords such as pardes, ‘park’ (2:5), and think the Solomonic voice in chapters 1 and 2 is a literary persona. Some conservative scholars, such as Duane Garrett, have continued to defend Solomonic authorship. The book's place in the canon was itself debated: the Mishnah (Yadayim 3:5) records rabbinic disagreement about whether Ecclesiastes ‘defiles the hands’, the rabbinic way of saying a book is Scripture, and the Talmud (Shabbat 30b) records the view that the sages wished to withdraw it because it contradicts itself, but kept it because it begins and ends with words of Torah.

The three Wisdom Books are best read together, because they argue with one another, and the canon keeps the argument rather than resolving it. Proverbs describes the moral order of a world God made: in general, wisdom leads to life and folly to ruin, diligence to plenty and laziness to want. Job insists that the general rule has painful exceptions, that a righteous man can suffer terribly for reasons no one on earth can see, and that applying the rule to every case is itself a kind of folly, one that can wound the suffering and misrepresent God. Ecclesiastes insists that human beings cannot see the whole, that death levels every achievement, and that the fitting response is reverent fear, honest limits, and grateful enjoyment of the gifts of each day.

It is easy to read the three as contradictory. It is better to read them as a mature account of wisdom in three voices. Proverbs without Job becomes a prosperity formula; Job without Proverbs becomes a counsel of despair about any moral order at all; both without Ecclesiastes forget that human understanding has limits and that life is short. All three share the same foundation. Proverbs begins with the fear of the LORD; Job's poem on wisdom ends with it: “the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding” (Job 28:28); Ecclesiastes concludes with it (12:13).

The Psalms carry the same debate. Psalm 1 sounds like Proverbs: the righteous flourish like a well-watered tree. Psalm 73 sounds like Job and Qohelet: “I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked.” (Psalm 73:3), until the psalmist enters the sanctuary and sees their end. Jesus himself steps into this conversation when he refuses to read disaster as a verdict on its victims, asking of those killed by the tower of Siloam, “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem?” (Luke 13:4), and when he tells his disciples that a man's blindness was not caused by his sin or his parents' (John 9:2-3).

In Proverbs 8, Wisdom speaks as a person who was with God before creation, present when he set the heavens in place, rejoicing in his world and delighting in humankind. Later Jewish writers developed the figure further. Ben Sira identified Wisdom with the Law of Moses (Sirach 24), and the Wisdom of Solomon describes her as a breath of God's power and a reflection of eternal light (Wisdom 7:25-26). Most scholars think Proverbs 8 is a personification, a poetic way of speaking of God's own wisdom, rather than the description of a separate divine being.

The New Testament writers drew on this language to speak of Christ. Paul calls Christ “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24) and says that in him are hidden “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). The descriptions of Christ as the agent of creation in John 1:1-3, Colossians 1:15-17, and Hebrews 1:2-3 use language close to what Jewish writers said of Wisdom. Jesus presents himself as more than a sage: “One greater than Solomon is here” (Matthew 12:42).

Proverbs 8 became a battleground in the fourth-century Arian controversy. The Septuagint of 8:22 has Wisdom say that the Lord ‘created’ her, and Arius and his followers took this as proof that the Son was a created being. The Hebrew verb, qanah, more often means to acquire or possess, and translations still differ (the Berean Standard Bible has “The LORD created me as His first course”). Athanasius and other defenders of the Nicene faith answered that Proverbs 8 is poetry about God's wisdom, that the verse should not be pressed into a statement about the Son's origin, and that where it is applied to Christ it speaks of his taking on created human nature. The church's confession at Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381), that the Son is begotten, not made, was reached partly through this argument over how to read a wisdom poem.

For the Christian reader, then, the Wisdom Books do several things at once. They teach the practical art of living well in God's world, much of which needs no translation across the centuries. They refuse easy answers to suffering and to the limits of human knowledge. And they point toward a wisdom that is finally personal, one that the New Testament finds in a crucified Messiah, whom Paul calls wisdom of a kind the world did not expect (1 Corinthians 1:18-25).

sections.h: How the Wisdom Books have been read
sections.body:
The Wisdom Books have a long history in Jewish and Christian reading. Gregory the Great's vast commentary on Job, the Moralia in Job (completed about 595), read the book on literal, allegorical, and moral levels and became one of the most copied works of the Middle Ages. Moses Maimonides discussed Job in his Guide for the Perplexed (twelfth century) as a meditation on providence. John Calvin preached 159 sermons on Job in Geneva in 1554 and 1555. In modern times Job has drawn writers outside the church as well as inside it: Søren Kierkegaard wrote about Job in Repetition (1843), Carl Jung published his provocative Answer to Job in 1952, and Archibald MacLeish's verse play J.B. (1958) retold the story in modern dress.

Ecclesiastes is read in synagogues at the Feast of Tabernacles (Sukkot), the autumn harvest festival, where its sober reflections on the brevity of life sit alongside the command to rejoice. Its lines have entered common speech, from ‘nothing new under the sun’ to ‘a time to be born, and a time to die’, and its third chapter has been set to music many times. Proverbs has shaped moral instruction in homes and schools for centuries.

The best way to read these books is slowly. A proverb is meant to be turned over, remembered, and applied in the right moment, not read at speed in a list. Job is best read whole, including the friends' speeches that readers are tempted to skip, because their failure is part of the lesson. Ecclesiastes is best read as a whole argument, with attention to where the frame voice speaks. And all three are best read in light of each other, so that each corrects the misuse of the others.
